searchText: Has anyone looked into front-running strategies post EIP-1559? Most miners just sort by highest gas price, so it's easy for frontrunners to compete to be the first while in the mempool, but I wonder if it will be the same post EIP-1559. Right now miners probably extract *some* of the revenue from the frontrunning that pay high gas prices, but curious what will happen post EIP-1559 I guess that's tightly related to implementation, which probably won't change on that aspect <@278762485497069569> unless miners change their sorting algorithm, front running will be the same. As long as miners decide order, front running will be a bribery game. Yes I understand, but the only reason why they would keep this sorting algorithm is for when blocks would hit the 20M limit, which I guess is a sufficient reason to keep things the same, in case it happens, but still may be faster for them not to do any sorting since most of the time they can just execute all txs in the mempool that have enough basefee + min tip I suspect that the sort itself is dirt cheap compared to most of the work miners do. Most likely indeed It seems like unnecessary added complexity to have something like: ```ts if (transactions.filter(eligible).sum(tx => tx.gas) > block.gasLimit * 2) { transactions.sort() } ```instead of just ```ts transactions.sort() ``` Though, it *would* be cool to break front runners so I would support mining nodes adding that in just to screw with them. 😀 Though, I suspect you'll end up with front running becoming a game of hashing power then, unless miners store transactions in a FIFO array. Actually, I think miners would prefer a client that actively supports front-running, since that can be a money maker. Miners already provide this service. Which service? they already support side channel payment for block inclusion. How does one contact a miner in order to get special inclusion? I haven't seen it advertised anywhere, and this doesn't feel like a feature that would need to be kept undergound. I think the fear of "miners will collude to drive base-fee to 0 so they can force first price auction" could be addressed by increasing the elasticity from 2x to say 4x or 5x or whatever we think clients can reasonably handle. Average gas used per second would remain at 10M on average, but we would allow bigger bursts. I personally am not worried about that type of collusion, but I also think that increasing elasticity is generally a positive thing up until we reach the threshold where client software starts choking due to single-block-size.
